questions.stem:
1. Researchers investigated whether introducing a good-luck-related superstition would improve the performance of participants attempting to hit a golf ball into a hole (Damisch, Stoberock, & Mussweiler, 2010). Participants in the study were randomly assigned to one of two groups. Those in the first group were told, “Here is your ball. So far it has turned out to be a lucky ball.” Those in the second group were told, “This is the ball everyone has used so far.” Participants then made ten attempts to hit the ball into the hole. The researchers measured the number of successful attempts, and they found that the mean difference between the two groups was statistically significant. The researchers theorized that the superstitious beliefs produced higher levels of self-efficacy, which led to improved performance.

Part A
Identify the design feature that makes the study experimental rather than correlational.
Explain what it means to say that there is a statistically significant difference between the two groups.
Explain how a superstitious belief might be related to a higher level of self-efficacy.

Part B
Many people engage in superstitious behavior, such as wearing lucky socks, in the belief that the superstitious behavior will lead to improved performance. Explain how each of the following may lead to the development or maintenance of superstitious beliefs or behaviors.
• Illusory correlation
• Positive reinforcement
• External locus of control
• Episodic memory
notes: Prompt transcribed from assets/psychology/papers/2016/2016.pdf.
Rubric parts were structured from the official scoring guidelines; no rubric points were invented.

questions.stem:
2. Part A
The vast majority of students in a prestigious engineering program are men. Some professors in the program hope to recruit and admit more women. How might each of the following hinder their decision-making process to accept more women?
• Representativeness heuristic
• Belief perseverance
• Group polarization

Part B
The program has an entrance exam that has been used for many years, but now the professors are considering eliminating it. How might each of the following affect the decision to eliminate the exam?
• Stereotype threat
• Predictive validity

Part C
The professors decide to start a summer internship for female high school students, which they hope will promote interest in their engineering program. How might each of the following be used in the internship to help recruit more female students?
• Extrinsic motivation
• Modeling
notes: Prompt transcribed from assets/psychology/papers/2016/2016.pdf.
Rubric parts were structured from the official scoring guidelines; no rubric points were invented.

frq_rubrics.general_considerations:
1. Answers must be presented in sentences, and sentences must be cogent enough for the student’s meaning to come through. Spelling and grammatical mistakes do not reduce a student’s score, but spelling must be close enough that the reader is convinced of the word.
2. Do not score students' notes made on the question section of the booklet. Score only what has been written in the blanks provided in the booklet.
3. Definitions alone will not score, but they may be used to enhance the application.
4. Within a point, a student will not be penalized for misinformation unless it directly contradicts correct information that would otherwise have scored a point. A correct application with incorrect definition is not considered a direct contradiction and should score the point.
5. Rubric examples provided for each point are not to be considered exhaustive.
6. A student can score points only if the student clearly conveys what part of the question is being answered. It is possible to infer the part of the question being answered if it is consistent with the order of the question.
7. The appropriate context of each section (A and B) must be explicitly established or related back to the prompt of the question.

parts.label: Point 1
parts.title: Experimental design
parts.criteria: The response identifies a design feature that makes the study experimental: participants were randomly assigned to one of two conditions, or the independent variable was manipulated. A complete description of the manipulation procedure scores even if the word “manipulation” is not used.
examples_positive: Participants were randomly assigned to the “Lucky Ball Group” or the other group.
The experimental group, the one receiving the treatment, was told they had the lucky ball.
The control group was not told that their ball had any lucky properties.
examples_negative: Random selection and random sampling do not score.
Simply stating that there was a control group does not score.

parts.label: Point 2
parts.title: Statistical significance
parts.criteria: The difference between the groups is less likely to be due to chance, random variation, coincidence, or Type I error; or it is more likely to be due to manipulation of the independent variable.
examples_positive: The researchers were 95% sure that the independent variable caused the difference between the groups.
The difference was not due to chance.
examples_negative: Using p < .05 alone does not score.

parts.label: Point 3
parts.title: Superstitious belief and self-efficacy
parts.criteria: Superstitious beliefs boost one’s belief that they can master a task or increase their personal skill level or capability. The increased confidence must reside within the person, not be ascribed to the ball.
examples_positive: Believing that one had the lucky ball led to greater certainty that they would get more balls into the hole.
examples_negative: Self-esteem definitions alone do not score.
References only to improved performance do not score.

parts.label: Point 4
parts.title: Illusory correlation
parts.criteria: The response must mention that a relationship is perceived and that the relationship is noncontingent, coincidental, false, or occurring by chance.
examples_positive: Jordan wears purple socks to a game and has a great game, then incorrectly assumes the socks caused the success.

parts.label: Point 5
parts.title: Positive reinforcement
parts.criteria: The response must reference performing a random/superstitious behavior, a desirable stimulus or outcome following that behavior, and an increased likelihood of the behavior occurring in the future.
examples_positive: I wore my purple socks and my team won; now I wear my purple socks for every game.
examples_negative: Strengthening the superstitious belief alone does not score; the behavior must be strengthened.

parts.label: Point 6
parts.title: External locus of control
parts.criteria: External circumstances—such as a powerful entity, chance, or luck—are believed to influence a logically unrelated result. Locus of control may be treated as a state or a trait.
examples_positive: Believing that lucky socks caused a good grade reflects an external locus of control.
examples_negative: Stating “external” alone without identifying a source of control does not score.

parts.label: Point 7
parts.title: Episodic memory
parts.criteria: The response must reference an individual’s memory, recall, or remembering of a specific personal event and connect it to superstitious beliefs or behaviors.
examples_positive: You recall only the baseball games in which you hit home runs while wearing purple socks, so you wear them for every game.

notes: Official scoring guidelines; points are 0/1.

1. Answers must be presented in sentences, and sentences must be cogent enough for the student’s meaning to come through. Spelling and grammatical mistakes do not reduce a student’s score, but spelling must be close enough that the reader is convinced of the word.
2. Do not score students' notes made on the question section of the booklet. Score only what has been written in the blanks provided in the booklet.

4. Within a particular point, a student will not be penalized for misinformation unless it directly contradicts correct information that would otherwise have scored a point. A correct application with incorrect definition is not considered a direct contradiction and should score the point.

parts.label: Point 1
parts.title: Representativeness heuristic
parts.criteria: The response explains how a prototypical or stereotypical categorization hinders the professors’ decision to admit more women: more engineers are male, men have characteristics of an engineer, or women lack those characteristics.
examples_positive: Women do not fit the prototype or stereotype of an engineer held by the admissions committee, so admission is harder.
examples_negative: Only describing the availability heuristic does not score.

parts.label: Point 2
parts.title: Belief perseverance
parts.criteria: The response must include an existing belief, evidence to the contrary, maintenance of the original belief, and hindrance of the decision to admit more women.
examples_positive: If the professors believe men are more competent engineers, they adhere to that belief even when disconfirming data show women are equally likely to succeed.

parts.label: Point 3
parts.title: Group polarization
parts.criteria: After discussion, the group consensus—not an individual’s view—becomes more extreme, and this hinders the professors’ decision to admit more women.
examples_positive: If the professors believe men are more competent, discussion makes the group’s conviction stronger and reduces women’s chances of admission.
examples_negative: Conformity or persuasion alone does not score.
A subgroup merely switching sides does not score.
Examples that relate only to groupthink do not score.

parts.label: Point 4
parts.title: Stereotype threat
parts.criteria: The response must address knowledge of a negative cultural stereotype that lowers expectations about ability, the resulting impairment of performance, and the impact on the decision to eliminate the exam.
examples_positive: Female applicants know the cultural assumption that men make better engineers, become anxious, and score lower; the professors then discontinue the exam.

parts.label: Point 5
parts.title: Predictive validity
parts.criteria: The response must show that a useful test is correlated with later performance on what it was designed to measure, and relate the direction of that relationship to the decision to keep or eliminate the exam.
examples_positive: Students who score well on the admissions exam also do well in coursework, so the committee keeps the exam.
Students who score poorly on the exam do well in the program, so the committee discontinues the exam.
parts.notes: High predictive validity contributes to keeping the exam; low predictive validity contributes to eliminating it.

parts.label: Point 6
parts.title: Extrinsic motivation
parts.criteria: An outside influence—a reward, reinforcement, or incentive—increases the recruitment of women into the program or internship.
examples_positive: A scholarship offered to all female students who complete the summer internship motivates more women to enroll.
examples_negative: The word “external” or “extrinsic” alone, without a reward or incentive linked to recruitment, does not score.

parts.label: Point 7
parts.title: Modeling
parts.criteria: The response must describe observing a behavior or a description of a behavior, acting in a similar manner by imitating or mimicking it, and increased female enrollment or interest.
examples_positive: Female engineers serve as mentors in the internship, giving high school students a role model to emulate and increasing their interest in engineering.
parts.notes: Joining the program or demonstrating interest fulfills both the imitation and increased-interest elements.

notes: Official scoring guidelines; points are 0/1.
